rationale: A wins because it knows where the cliff edge is and stops before tumbling over it. Its strongest line, "Databricks says revenue run rate passed $3B, growing 60%, with an IPO still undated," keeps the markets angle honest. B has real bones, but "Why would a company chasing an IPO give away its flagship AI model?" stuffs two unsupported adjectives into one headline and calls it strategy. That is how a decent angle gets dressed for a TED panel and mugged by a fact-checker.
gaps_in_A: "Why a company with $3B in revenue is giving its foundation model away" leans on "giving away" before the license terms prove how open or free the release really is.
"buyers who cannot send data outside their own environment" is plausible, but still inferred from regulated-enterprise positioning rather than directly supplied in the update.
The third angle is smart but fragile: it admits "this collapses back into the first angle" without a real explanation of how the open model drives revenue.
gaps_in_B: "$3B ARR disclosure" is not in the update. The fact supplied was "$3B in annualized revenue"; ARR is a more specific metric and you don't get to upgrade it for drama.
"flagship AI model" is invented. The update says new foundation model, not flagship, core product, or most valuable IP.
"company chasing an IPO" overcooks "has signaled an eventual IPO without a date." That is not a chase; that is a breadcrumb.
"finance, healthcare, insurance" are plausible regulated examples, but no specific verticals were supplied. Use them as examples carefully or don't use them.
